title: Reusable Magnetic Material Removes Over 95% of Microplastics and PFAS From Water
excerpt: An RMIT University team has upgraded its 2022 magnetic powder to capture nanoplastics, PFAS and heavy metals in one hour, with industry partners now preparing the technology for real-world deployment.
body:
• RMIT University researchers developed a magnetic adsorbent that removes over 95% of micro- and nanoplastics from water within one hour, including particles as small as 30 nanometres.
  • The material also captures PFAS compounds, mercury, chromium, copper, dyes and ibuprofen at similar removal rates.
  • Manufacturing costs have dropped roughly 75% since the team's 2022 breakthrough, and the material can be recovered magnetically and reused multiple times.
  • Industry partnerships in Canada, Australia and the United States — including in California, where microplastic regulations are tightening — signal a path toward commercial deployment.

Researchers at Australia's RMIT University have developed a reusable magnetic material that strips more than 95 per cent of micro- and nanoplastics from water in a single hour, according to a study published this month in the Chemical Engineering Journal.

The invention builds on the team's 2022 breakthrough, which first demonstrated that iron-containing nanomaterials could attract microplastics and be pulled out of water with a magnet. The updated material goes further, capturing plastic particles as small as 30 nanometres — far below the detection threshold of conventional wastewater treatment plants — while also removing PFAS compounds, heavy metals and pharmaceutical residues.

How it works

The adsorbent is a dark, powdery substance built on a metal-organic framework, or MOF, structure. When mixed into contaminated water, its engineered surface binds to plastic particles, dissolved pollutants and emerging contaminants. Because the material contains iron, a magnet can then separate the loaded adsorbent from treated water in seconds.

"Our material is designed to remove micro- and nano-plastics quickly."

— Dr Muhammad Haris, RMIT School of Engineering

In laboratory tests, the material removed over 95 per cent of tested contaminants including mercury, chromium, copper, dyes and ibuprofen. About 80 per cent of pollutants were captured in the first 15 minutes — a timeline that aligns with contact times used in existing treatment plants. The material performed consistently across common plastics such as polyethylene, polypropylene and polyester, and in both fresh and saline water.

From laboratory to laundry wastewater

To test real-world viability, the team ran the material through industrial laundry wastewater, a major source of synthetic microfibre pollution. It removed more than 88 per cent of polyester microfibres along with dyes, maintaining performance despite the presence of surfactants and organic matter.

A prototype system combining the adsorbent with magnetic separation technology from Canadian company One Eye Industries demonstrated that the material could be recovered quickly and reused after treatment.

"Industry has been waiting for a practical way to move microplastics and emerging contaminants removal out of the laboratory and into real treatment environments. The challenge isn't only capturing these particles, it's recovering the treatment material quickly and reliably after it has done its job, without creating a new waste stream."

— Roger Simonson, founder, One Eye Industries

Co-lead researcher Associate Professor Nasir Mahmood said the results supported practical deployment. "It worked in realistic water conditions, handled mixed pollutants and could be recovered efficiently," he said.

Cheaper to make, ready to scale

Since the 2022 version, the team has increased production output fivefold through a room-temperature manufacturing process that uses fewer costly inputs. Early analysis suggests costs have dropped by about 75 per cent compared to earlier versions. The material can also be reused multiple times, further reducing operational costs.

"Our goal was to make the technology effective, practical and affordable at scale," said lead researcher Professor Nicky Eshtiaghi. "This includes ensuring the material can be recovered, reused and integrated into existing treatment systems."

Industry partnerships and regulatory pressure

RMIT is partnering with Indigenous-owned Fire and Test Australasia in Geelong, Victoria, to explore applications in stormwater and community wastewater treatment. The team is also collaborating with Star Water Group, an Australian company with clients in the United States, including California, where tightening regulations are increasing demand for microplastics treatment.

Governments in Europe and the US are placing stricter limits on microplastics entering waterways, creating commercial urgency. The dual-use capability — capturing both microplastics and PFAS, the so-called "forever chemicals" — could give the technology a competitive edge in markets where both pollutants are under regulatory scrutiny.

A broader wave of innovation

RMIT's magnetic material is part of a wider push to tackle microplastic pollution using novel approaches. In a separate study published this month in ACS ES&T Water, another RMIT team led by Associate Professor Biplob Pramanik showed that combining microbubbles and nanobubbles in existing wastewater treatment systems could remove more than 90 per cent of microplastics — reaching 97 per cent for polystyrene — without major infrastructure changes.

Meanwhile, South African researchers published findings in October 2025 showing that magnetic nanocomposites made from carbon and boron nitride sheets removed up to 96 per cent of microplastics from drinking water and municipal wastewater, at a cost of about $41 per 1,000 litres.

For the Indian diaspora, the developments carry particular relevance. India's rivers face severe microplastic contamination, and affordable, scalable treatment technologies could have outsized impact in the subcontinent's water infrastructure. California, home to one of the largest Indian American populations, is among the US jurisdictions tightening microplastic standards — meaning these technologies may soon affect water quality in communities where many Indian families live.
nri_angle: India faces severe microplastic contamination in its waterways, and California — home to a large Indian American population — is tightening microplastic regulations, making affordable magnetic treatment technologies directly relevant to diaspora communities.
